input.question: Why does a hearing a recording of my voice sound different to me then when I hear myself talk?
input.ground_truth: We hear sounds as vibrations hitting our ear drums. When we hear most sounds, these vibrations travel through the air and into the ear canal. Our own voices also vibrate through our bodies, creating a slightly lower pitch. When you hear a recording of your voice you are missing this extra level of vibration that lowers the sound, so your voice sounds higher than what you are used to. Source: _URL_0_

response.prediction: When you speak, your voice reaches your ears in two ways: through the air as sound waves (like others hear it) and through vibrations that travel directly through your bones and skull (bone conduction). These bone vibrations add depth and richness to your own voice, making it sound deeper and more resonant to you. However, when you hear a recording, it only captures the sound waves traveling through the air, missing the bone-conducted part. This makes your recorded voice sound higher-pitched, thinner, or less familiar, because it lacks the internal resonance you’re used to hearing. That’s why your voice often sounds different on recordings—it’s simply missing the extra bass frequencies your body naturally adds.
